column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 22: “Will I enter Paradise?”

column2: From Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh (may Allah be pleased with them both): A man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying:
Tell me: if I pray the obligatory prayers, fast Ramaḍān, treat the lawful as lawful and the unlawful as unlawful, and add nothing to that, will I enter Paradise? He said: “Yes.” Muslim reported it.
Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Abū al-Zubayr from Jābir, adding at its end: He said: By Allah, I will add nothing to that.

He also recorded it through the narration of al-Aʿmash, from Abū Ṣāliḥ and Abū Sufyān, from Jābir, who said: Al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal said: Messenger of Allah, tell me: if I pray the obligatory prayer, treat the unlawful as unlawful and the lawful as lawful, and add nothing to that, will I enter Paradise?
The Prophet ﷺ said: “Yes.”

Some have explained “treating the lawful as lawful” as believing it to be lawful, and “treating the unlawful as unlawful” as believing it to be unlawful while avoiding it. It may also be that “treating the lawful as lawful” means doing it, “the lawful” here referring to whatever is not unlawful,

so that it takes in what is obligatory, recommended and permissible. The meaning would then be that he does what is not forbidden to him, does not go beyond what has been permitted to him to something else, and avoids what is unlawful.

It has been narrated from a number of the Salaf, among them Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās, that they said concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic, “Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited; it is they who believe in it” [al-Baqarah 2:121]: They treat what it makes lawful as lawful and what it makes unlawful as unlawful, and do not distort it from its proper places.
What is meant by treating as lawful and as unlawful is doing what is lawful and avoiding what is unlawful, as mentioned in this hadith.

Allah the Exalted said concerning the disbelievers who used to alter the sanctity of the sacred months: “Postponing [a sacred month] is only an increase in disbelief, by which those who disbelieve are led astray. They make it lawful one year and unlawful another year, to match the number that Allah has made sacred, and so make lawful what Allah has made unlawful” [al-Tawbah 9:37].
What is meant is that one year they would fight in the sacred month, thereby treating it as lawful, and another year they would refrain from fighting in it, thereby treating it as sacred.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “O you who believe, do not make unlawful the good things Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress; indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors. And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good” [al-Māʾidah 5:87–88]. This verse was revealed because of some people who refrained from partaking of certain good things out of detachment from the world and austerity.
Some of them had made that unlawful for themselves, either by an oath they swore or by declaring it unlawful for themselves — none of which makes it unlawful in reality —

and some of them refrained from it without any oath or declaration. Allah called all of this “making unlawful”, since they meant by refraining from it to inflict hardship on themselves and hold their souls back from their desires.
It is said proverbially: So-and-so neither treats things as lawful nor as unlawful — meaning that he does not refrain from doing what is unlawful and does not stop at what has been permitted to him,
even if he believes the unlawful to be unlawful. Thus people regard whoever does what is unlawful and does not shrink from it as treating it as lawful, even if he does not believe it to be lawful.

In any case, this hadith shows that whoever fulfils the obligations and refrains from what is forbidden will enter Paradise. Hadiths with this meaning, or something close to it, have come from the Prophet ﷺ in great numbers. Thus al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān
and al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah and Abū Saʿīd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no servant who prays the five prayers, fasts Ramaḍān, pays the zakāh

and avoids the seven major sins, but the gates of Paradise are opened for him, and he may enter by whichever he wishes.” Then he recited: “If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will expiate your misdeeds for you” [al-Nisāʾ 4:31].

Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever worships Allah without associating anything with Him, establishes the prayer, pays the zakāh, fasts Ramaḍān and avoids the major sins will have Paradise” — or: “will enter Paradise.”

In the Musnad, from Ibn ʿAbbās: Ḍimām ibn Thaʿlabah came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ, and he mentioned to him the five prayers, fasting, zakāh, Ḥajj and all the laws of Islam. When he had finished, Ḍimām said:

I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah. I will fulfil these obligations and avoid what you have forbidden me, neither adding nor taking away. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “If he is truthful, he will enter Paradise.”

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it by another route, and in his narration Ḍimām said: As for the fifth, I have no desire for it — meaning indecent acts. Then he said: I will certainly act on them, I and whoever obeys me. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “If he is truthful, he will surely enter Paradise.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Abū Ayyūb: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: Tell me of a deed that will admit me to Paradise. He said: “Worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the prayer, pay the zakāh and maintain ties of kinship.”
Muslim recorded it too, except that in his version the man said: Tell me of a deed that will bring me near to Paradise and keep me far from the Fire.
In one of his narrations: When the man turned away, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “If he holds to what he has been commanded, he will enter Paradise.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah: A Bedouin said: Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed by which, if I do it, I will enter Paradise. He said: “Worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the obligatory prayer, pay the obligatory zakāh

and fast Ramaḍān.” The man said: By the One who sent you with the truth, I will never add anything to this, nor take anything from it. When he turned away, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever would be glad to look at a man of the people of Paradise, let him look at this man.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbaydillāh: A Bedouin with dishevelled hair came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: Messenger of Allah, tell me what prayer Allah has made obligatory on me.
He said: “The five prayers — unless you do something voluntarily.” He said: Tell me what fasting Allah has made obligatory on me.
He said: “The month of Ramaḍān — unless you do something voluntarily.” He said: Tell me what zakāh Allah has made obligatory on me.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ told him the laws of Islam, and he said: By the One who has honoured you with the truth, I will do nothing voluntary, and I will not fall short in anything Allah has made obligatory on me.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “He has succeeded, if he is truthful” — or: “He will enter Paradise, if he is truthful.” The wording is al-Bukhārī's.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Anas: A Bedouin asked the Prophet ﷺ — and he mentioned it with the same meaning, adding:

“Pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it.” The man said: By the One who sent you with the truth, I will not add to them nor take from them. The Prophet ﷺ said: “If he is truthful, he will surely enter Paradise.”

What the Bedouin meant was that he would add nothing voluntary to the obligatory prayer, the obligatory zakāh, the fast of Ramaḍān and the pilgrimage to the House; he did not mean that he would not act on any other of the laws and obligations of Islam. These hadiths do not mention avoiding what is forbidden,
because the questioner was asking only about the deeds by which the one who does them enters Paradise.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivering a sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage, saying: “O people, fear Allah, pray your five,

fast your month, pay the zakāh on your wealth and obey those in authority over you, and you will enter the Paradise of your Lord.” He said: ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Imam Aḥmad recorded it with “Worship your Lord” in place of “Fear Allah”.

Baqī ibn Makhlad recorded it in his Musnad by another route, the wording of his narration being: “Pray your five, fast your month, make pilgrimage to your House, and pay the zakāh on your wealth willingly, and you will enter the Paradise of your Lord.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, with his chain, from Ibn al-Muntafiq, who said: I came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was at ʿArafāt, and said: There are two things I want to ask you about: what will save me from the Fire, and what will admit me to Paradise?

He said: “Though you have put your question briefly, you have asked about something great and far-reaching. So understand from me: worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the obligatory prayer,
pay the obligatory zakāh and fast Ramaḍān. Whatever you would like people to do to you, do it to them; and whatever you would hate people to bring upon you, spare people from it.”

In another narration of his he said: “Fear Allah, do not associate anything with Him, establish the prayer, pay the zakāh, make pilgrimage to the House and fast Ramaḍān, without adding anything to that.” It has been said that this Companion was the delegate of Banū al-Muntafiq, and that his name was Laqīṭ.

These deeds, then, are causes that bring about entry into Paradise, while committing forbidden acts may act as impediments. This is shown by what Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Murrah al-Juhanī,
who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Messenger of Allah, I have testified that there is no god but Allah

and that you are the Messenger of Allah; I have prayed the five, paid the zakāh on my wealth and fasted the month of Ramaḍān. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever dies upon this will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs on the Day of Resurrection, like this” — and he held up his two fingers — “so long as he is not undutiful to his parents.”

Entry into Paradise has also been made consequent on doing some of these deeds, such as prayer. In the well-known hadith: “Whoever prays the prayers at their times has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise.”

In the authentic hadith: “Whoever prays the two cool prayers [Fajr and ʿAṣr] will enter Paradise.” All this is a matter of mentioning the cause that brings something about, which has its effect only when all its conditions are met and its impediments are absent.

This is shown by what Imam Aḥmad recorded from Bashīr ibn al-Khaṣāṣiyah, who said: I came to the Prophet ﷺ to pledge allegiance to him, and he made it a condition for me that I testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger, that I establish the prayer, pay the zakāh,

perform the Ḥajj of Islam, fast Ramaḍān and fight in the path of Allah. I said: Messenger of Allah, as for two of them, by Allah I cannot manage them: jihād and charity. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ closed his hand, then shook it, and said: “No jihād and no charity?
Then by what will you enter Paradise?”
I said: Messenger of Allah, I will pledge allegiance to you. And I pledged allegiance to him on all of them.
This hadith shows that these qualities are not enough to enter Paradise without zakāh and jihād.

It is established in authentic hadiths that committing certain major sins prevents entry into Paradise, such as his words: “One who severs ties of kinship will not enter Paradise”; “No one will enter Paradise who has an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart”; and “You will not enter Paradise until you believe,

and you will not believe until you love one another.” So too the hadiths that have come about debt barring entry into Paradise until it is repaid; and in the Ṣaḥīḥ: “When the believers have crossed the Bridge, they will be detained on a span (qanṭarah), where they will be made to settle the wrongs that were between them in this world.”
One of the Salaf said: A man may be held at the gate of Paradise for a hundred years because of a sin he used to commit in this world.
All of these are impediments.
From this the meaning of the hadiths that make entry into Paradise consequent on tawḥīd alone becomes clear. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Dharr,
the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no servant who says, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and then dies upon that, but he will enter Paradise.” I said: Even if he commits adultery and steals?!

He said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals.” He said it three times, and then said on the fourth: “Even if Abū Dharr's nose be rubbed in the dust.” Abū Dharr went out saying: Even if Abū Dharr's nose be rubbed in the dust.
Both also have, from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever testifies that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger,

and that ʿĪsā is the servant of Allah and His Messenger, His word which He cast to Maryam and a spirit from Him, and that Paradise is true and the Fire is true, Allah will admit him to Paradise, whatever his deeds may have been.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah or Abū Saʿīd — the narrator being unsure which — the Prophet ﷺ said:
“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. No servant meets Allah with these two, free of doubt, and is then barred from Paradise.”

It also has, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said to him one day: “Whomever you meet who testifies that there is no god but Allah, his heart certain of it, give him glad tidings of Paradise.” There are very many hadiths with this meaning.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said one day to Muʿādh: “There is no servant who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger but Allah makes him forbidden to the Fire.”
Both also have, from ʿItbān ibn Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has made forbidden to the Fire whoever says ‘There is no god but Allah’, seeking by it the Face of Allah.”

A group of scholars said: The word of tawḥīd is a cause that brings about entry into Paradise and salvation from the Fire, but it has conditions, which are fulfilling the obligations, and impediments, which are committing major sins.
Al-Ḥasan said to al-Farazdaq: “There is no god but Allah” has conditions, so beware of slandering a chaste woman.

It is related that he also said: This is the pole — so where are the tent-ropes? That is, the word of tawḥīd is the tent's central pole, but the tent will not stand without its ropes, which are doing the obligations and leaving what is forbidden.

Al-Ḥasan was told: Some people say that whoever says “There is no god but Allah” will enter Paradise. He said: Whoever says “There is no god but Allah” and fulfils its right and its obligation will enter Paradise.
Wahb ibn Munabbih was asked: Is not “There is no god but Allah” the key to Paradise? He said: Certainly;
but every key has teeth. If you bring a key that has teeth, it will open for you; otherwise it will not open for you.
Similar to this is what is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar: he was asked whether, with “There is no god but Allah”, any deed could do harm, just as no deed benefits when it is abandoned.
Ibn ʿUmar said: Live, and do not be deceived.

Another group, among them al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Zuhrī, said: This was before the obligations and the prescribed punishments were laid down. Some of them indicated that it was abrogated; others said that conditions were joined to it and added. Whether adding a condition counts as abrogation or not
is a well-known point of disagreement among the scholars of legal theory. All of this is open to question, for many of these hadiths came late, after the obligations and the prescribed punishments.

Al-Thawrī said: The obligations and the prescribed punishments abrogated them. He may have meant what those others meant; or he may have meant that the obligations and prescribed punishments, once made binding, made it clear that worldly punishments are not cancelled merely by the two testimonies of faith,

and so neither are the punishments of the Hereafter. The Salaf used to call this kind of clarification and removal of a false impression “abrogation” (naskh), though it is not abrogation in the well-known technical sense.

Another group said: These unqualified texts have come qualified elsewhere by the condition that one says it truthfully and sincerely, and saying it sincerely and truthfully rules out persisting in sin alongside it.
Among the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever says ‘There is no god but Allah’ sincerely will enter Paradise.” He was asked: What is its sincerity?
He said: “That it holds you back from what Allah has forbidden.”
This has also been narrated with a connected chain by other routes, which are weak.

Perhaps al-Ḥasan was pointing to this in the words of his that we related earlier. For when the heart truly realises the meaning of “There is no god but Allah”, and is truthful and sincere in it, this requires that devotion to Allah alone as God become firmly rooted in it — in reverence,

awe, fear, love, hope, veneration and reliance — and fill it, and that devotion to any created thing besides Him as a god be banished from it. When that is so, there remains in it no love, no will and no seeking of anything other than what Allah wills, loves and seeks;

and thereby all the whims and wishes of the soul, and the whisperings of Satan, are banished from the heart. Whoever loves a thing and obeys it, and loves and hates for its sake, has made it his god. So whoever loves and hates only for Allah, and befriends and opposes only for His sake,

has Allah truly as his god; and whoever loves and hates, befriends and opposes for the sake of his whim, has his whim as his god, as the Exalted said: “Have you seen the one who takes his own whim as his god?” [al-Jāthiyah 45:23]. Al-Ḥasan said: He is the one who never desires anything without going after it.
Qatādah said: He is the one who, whenever he desires a thing, goes after it, and whenever he craves something, takes it, with no scrupulousness or taqwā to hold him back.

It is narrated as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ), from the hadith of Abū Umāmah: “Under the shade of the sky there is no god worshipped that is greater in Allah's sight than a whim that is followed.”

Likewise, whoever obeys Satan in disobedience to Allah has worshipped him, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Did I not enjoin upon you, children of Ādam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you” [Yā Sīn 36:60].
It is clear from this that one can truly realise the meaning of saying “There is no god but Allah” only if there is in one's heart no persistence in loving what Allah dislikes
or in wanting what Allah does not want. Whenever there is anything of this in the heart, it is a deficiency in tawḥīd and a kind of hidden shirk.
That is why Mujāhid said concerning the words of the Exalted, “that you associate nothing with Him” [al-Anʿām 6:151]: Do not love anyone other than Me.
In the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Ḥākim, from ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Shirk is more hidden than the creeping of ants on a smooth rock on a dark night,
and the least of it is that you love on account of something unjust, or hate on account of something just. Is religion anything other than love and hate?
Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ‘Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you’” [Āl ʿImrān 3:31].
This is an explicit text that loving what Allah dislikes and hating what He loves is following whim, and that befriending and opposing on that basis is hidden shirk.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded, from the hadith of Anas, as marfūʿ: “‘There is no god but Allah’ will continue to protect the servants from Allah's displeasure

so long as they do not prefer their worldly life to the bargain of their religion. When they prefer the bargain of their worldly life to their religion and then say ‘There is no god but Allah’, it is thrown back at them, and Allah says:
You have lied.”
This makes clear the meaning of his words ﷺ, “Whoever testifies that there is no god but Allah, truthfully from his heart, Allah makes him forbidden to the Fire,”

and that those of the people of this word who enter the Fire do so because of how little truthfulness they had in saying it. For when this word is truthful, it purifies the heart of everything besides Allah.
Whoever is truthful in saying “There is no god but Allah” loves none besides Him, hopes in none but Him, fears no one but Allah,

relies on none but Allah, and has no remnant left of the traces of his self and his whims. Whenever some trace of anything besides Allah remains in the heart, it is from a lack of truthfulness in saying it.

The fire of Hell is extinguished by the light of the faith of those who affirm Allah's oneness, as in the well-known hadith: “The Fire will say to the believer: Pass on, believer, for your light has put out my flame.”

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Jābir, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There will remain no righteous or wicked person but will enter it, and it will be coolness and safety for the believers as it was for Ibrāhīm — so much so that the Fire will cry out because of their coolness.”
This is an inheritance the believers have received from the state of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): the fire of Hell fears the fire of love in the believers' hearts.
Al-Junayd said: The Fire said: Lord, had I not obeyed You, would You have punished me with anything more severe than me?
He said: Yes, I would have set My greater fire upon you. It said: Is there any fire greater and more severe than me?
He said: Yes — the fire of My love, which I have made to dwell in the hearts of My believing friends.
On this, someone said:
In the lover's heart burns a fire of passion / whose coolest flame is Hell's hottest fire.

This meaning is attested by the hadith of Muʿādh, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever's last words are ‘There is no god but Allah’ will enter Paradise”; for a dying man hardly says it except with sincerity,
repentance, regret for what is past and resolve not to return to the like of it. Al-Khaṭṭābī preferred this view in a separate treatise of his on tawḥīd, and it is a good one.
